title: Big-O
short: Say how the work grows when the input gets bigger.
what: Big-O is a rough label for how much more work your code does as the input grows. It ignores the speed of your laptop and small details, and keeps only the shape: flat, slow climb, straight line, or explosion. n means the size of the input, like the length of a list.
analogy: Finding a name in a phone book. Reading every page grows with the book (O(n)); opening the middle and halving grows very slowly (O(log n)); comparing every name with every other name explodes (O(n²)).

frames.label: steps, roughly
frames.say: Each row is a way code can grow. Each column is a bigger input. Let's fill in roughly how many steps each one takes.

frames.label: steps, roughly
frames.say: With n = 1 item, every row costs about 1 step. Tiny inputs make all code look equally fast.

frames.label: steps, roughly
frames.say: At n = 10: one loop does 10 steps, a loop inside a loop does 100, and halving needs only 4.

frames.label: steps, roughly
frames.say: At n = 100 the gap opens: 7 steps for halving, 100 for one loop, 10,000 for a loop inside a loop.

frames.label: steps, roughly
frames.say: At n = 1000, O(n²) needs a million steps. O(log n) still needs only 10. The shape matters more than anything else.

frames.label: steps, roughly
frames.say: This is why interviews ask for Big-O: swapping a loop inside a loop for one loop turns 1,000,000 steps into 1,000.

when: Can you do better than O(n²)?
Will this still work for a million items?
What is the time and space complexity?
cost: Read nums[i] or a dict key
watch: Drop constants and small terms: 3n + 5 is still O(n).
Count memory too: building a new list of n items is O(n) space.
Hidden loops count: x in a_list, a_list.index(x) and slicing are each O(n).
